client: I've been really struggling this past week because I have this big presentation at an annual conference coming up, and after I completely blanked during practice yesterday, my anxiety has just been through the roof. I keep replaying that moment over and over in my head, and I can't stop thinking that I'm going to embarrass myself in front of everyone. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to fix anything, because the presentation is still happening whether I feel better about it or not.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot of tension right now, and that moment of blanking has really taken hold in your mind as "proof" of what's going to happen — which is such a common but painful thinking trap called *fortune-telling*. You're right that the presentation is happening regardless, and that's actually where we can focus our energy: not on eliminating the anxiety, but on loosening the grip that one practice moment has over how you see your abilities. What would you say to a colleague who blanked once during practice — would you take that as solid evidence they'd fail the real thing?

client: Honestly, if a colleague blanked during practice I'd probably just tell them it happens and not to worry about it. But it feels different when it's me — like I'm supposed to know this material better than anyone, and blanking feels like a sign that I actually don't. I get what you're saying about fortune-telling, but I'm not sure I can just flip a switch and stop believing what that moment felt like.
therapist: You've just noticed something really important — that you hold yourself to a completely different standard than you'd hold anyone else, which tells us the issue isn't really about the blanking itself, but about what you *believe* it means specifically for you. And you're absolutely right that insight alone doesn't instantly change how something *feels*; that's not how this works, and it's okay that it doesn't just "click" immediately. I'm curious — when you say you're supposed to know this material better than anyone, where does that expectation come from, and do you think it's one you'd ever actually consider fair if you examined it closely?

client: I guess the expectation comes from... I don't know, years of being the person everyone looked to for answers. Like, I built my whole identity around being competent and reliable, so when I blank like that in a presentation, it feels like the whole foundation just cracks. And honestly, when you ask if it's fair — I know logically it isn't, but knowing that doesn't stop it from feeling completely true in the moment.
therapist: What you're describing — your entire sense of self being tied to never faltering — is such a heavy thing to carry, and it makes complete sense that one moment of blanking would feel so destabilizing rather than just inconvenient. That gap you're noticing, between *knowing* something isn't fair and still *feeling* it as completely true, is actually one of the most important things we can work with in CBT — because it tells us the belief runs really deep, not that you're broken or beyond help. I'm wondering, can you think of a time in the past where you stumbled or felt uncertain, but your competence and reliability actually held up in the end anyway?

client: I mean... yeah, there was this one time about two years ago where I completely froze during a presentation at work, like my mind just went blank for what felt like forever. But I recovered, I kept going, and my manager actually came up to me afterward and said it was one of the clearer explanations of the project she'd heard. The thing is, even remembering that right now, I still feel this pull to dismiss it, like "okay but that was different" or "you just got lucky that time."
therapist: That memory is really significant — you froze, you recovered, and you were *told* it landed well, which is genuine evidence that your competence isn't as fragile as the anxiety wants you to believe. But notice what your mind just did automatically: it reached for "that was different" or "you got lucky," which is another thinking pattern called *discounting the positive*, where your brain works overtime to protect that core belief even when the facts challenge it. What do you think it would take for a success to actually "count" as real evidence of your ability — is there any version of this presentation going well that your mind *wouldn't* find a way to dismiss?

client: That question actually kind of stops me in my tracks, because honestly... I'm not sure there is a version. Like, if it goes perfectly, I'd probably think "okay but that was a fluke" or "the bar was just low," and if it goes badly, well, that confirms everything I already feared. It's like my mind has set it up so I literally cannot win, and saying that out loud makes me feel kind of hopeless about it.
therapist: The fact that you can see that pattern so clearly right now — that your mind has essentially built a system where no outcome can count as a win — is actually a really meaningful moment, not a reason to feel hopeless. What you've just described isn't a reflection of reality; it's a reflection of how ironclad that core belief about your identity has become, and the good news is that *seeing the trap* is genuinely the first step toward loosening it. I'm curious — if your sense of worth can't be earned back through any outcome of this presentation, do you think it's possible that your competence and value might need to rest on something that isn't so vulnerable to a single moment?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but I honestly don't know what else my worth would rest on if not things like this presentation. Like, if I strip away my performance at work, what's actually left that proves I'm not just... failing at being a person? It feels less like a trap and more like just the truth about me.
therapist: What you just said — "failing at being a person" — tells me this goes so much deeper than a presentation, and I want to gently stay with that for a moment, because that's a really painful place to be sitting. The fact that your worth feels like it *needs* to be proven, constantly, through performance, isn't the truth about you — it's actually a belief that was built over time, probably for very understandable reasons, and things that are built can be examined and slowly rebuilt differently. I'm wondering — in your life, are there people who care about you not because of what you deliver or achieve, but just because of *who you are*, and what do you make of that?

client: I mean... my sister, maybe. She checks in on me even when I haven't done anything impressive lately, just texts to see how I'm doing. But honestly, part of me always wonders if she's just being polite, or if she'd pull back if she really saw how much I'm struggling right now.
therapist: There's something really tender in the way you mentioned your sister — like a small, quiet part of you *wants* to let that in, but there's this protective instinct that rushes in to explain it away before it can actually land. It's worth noticing that this is the same pattern we've been talking about: your mind discounting evidence that doesn't fit the belief that you're fundamentally not enough. What do you think it would feel like — even just as an experiment — to let your sister's care be real and uncomplicated, without needing to find the catch?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to just... accept that, but it almost feels dangerous somehow, like if I let myself believe her care is real and uncomplicated, I'll lower my guard and then get hurt when it turns out I was wrong about her too. It's easier to find the catch ahead of time than to be blindsided later. I guess I don't fully trust that I'm someone worth caring about without conditions, so I keep looking for the fine print.
therapist: What you just described — scanning for the fine print before you can let anything good in — sounds like it's been a way of protecting yourself for a long time, and it makes a lot of sense that it developed, even if it's also quietly keeping you isolated. That belief, "I'm only worth caring about conditionally," is really at the heart of so much of what we've been talking about today, from the presentation anxiety all the way to your sister's texts. I'm wondering — can you recall a moment, maybe early on, where you first learned that love or care came with conditions attached?

client: Yeah... I think about my dad a lot when this comes up. He was proud of me when I did well in school, like genuinely warm and present, but when I struggled or made mistakes he'd just kind of go quiet and distant, not mean exactly, just... gone. I learned pretty early that the good version of him was something I had to earn, and I guess I've just been applying that math to everyone ever since.
therapist: What you just shared takes real courage, and it makes so much sense — a child who learned that warmth had to be *earned* and could be *lost* would absolutely grow up doing exactly what you've been doing, constantly performing, scanning for the fine print, never quite letting care feel safe. That "math," as you called it, wasn't a flaw in you; it was a very logical response to the emotional environment you grew up in, but you've been applying an old equation to people and situations that may not actually work that way. I'm curious — now that you can see where that belief came from, does it change anything about how you relate to it, even just a little?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually does feel something shift a little when you frame it that way — like, okay, maybe I wasn't just broken or paranoid, maybe it made sense given what I was working with. But then there's this other part of me that immediately goes, "so what, knowing where it came from doesn't make it feel any less true right now." Like, my brain still does the math automatically, even if I can see the equation written on the board.
therapist: That shift you felt, even briefly, actually matters more than it might seem — you're not trying to erase the equation overnight, you're just starting to notice that *you* are the one who learned it, which means you're not the same thing as the equation itself. You're absolutely right that insight doesn't rewire the automatic response immediately; that takes repetition and practice, much like how the original belief got reinforced over years of small moments with your dad. What do you think it might look like, in a small and manageable way, to start collecting new data points — moments where you let care or success count, just a little, without immediately looking for the catch?
